topics.title: The Iran war reaches the Strait of Hormuz
topics.hook: In May 2026 the war that began with the killing of Iran's Supreme Leader in February spread into the Strait of Hormuz, and the world found out again how one narrow waterway can move the price of everything.
topics.story:
The war started on 28 February 2026. Israel and the United States launched simultaneous operations, code-named Roaring Lion and Epic Fury, that killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and several senior commanders in a single night. The Israeli Air Force flew its largest combat sortie ever, hitting roughly 500 targets with over 1,200 bombs in 24 hours, and a cyberattack knocked out Iran's internet for more than 60 hours. Iran had been through a shorter round with Israel already, the Twelve-Day War of June 2025, which in hindsight looks like a rehearsal.

What followed was not a quick war. Iran struck back at Israel, the Gulf states and US bases. Hezbollah was drawn in from Lebanon. A two-week ceasefire opened on 8 April and fell apart within days; a round of talks in Islamabad on 12 and 13 April, with Pakistan's foreign minister Ishaq Dar shuttling between Washington and Tehran, produced nothing durable.

May is when the war reached the world's most important oil chokepoint. On 4 May, the US Navy launched Operation Project Freedom, escorting tankers through the Strait of Hormuz, the 33-kilometre-wide passage between Iran and Oman through which roughly a fifth of the world's traded oil moves. Iran's regular navy and its Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps navy treated the escorts as provocation. On 7 May, Iran fired on three US destroyers, USS Truxtun, USS Rafael Peralta and USS Mason; US Central Command answered with what it called self-defence strikes on Iranian military sites, and explosions were reported at the ports of Bandar Abbas and Qeshm. Washington insisted this was not a restart of full-scale war, a distinction that meant very little to shipping insurers, who priced Gulf transits as a war-risk zone through the month.

The casualty count by June, when a ceasefire finally held, ran into the thousands: Iran put its own dead at roughly 3,500 with over 26,000 injured, the US lost 19 soldiers and a contractor, and Israel recorded 38 soldiers and 31 civilians killed. Hezbollah alone reported over a thousand fighters dead.

India's stake in all this was never abstract. India imports more than four-fifths of its crude oil, and a large share of it moves through the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz on its way from Saudi Arabia, Iraq and the UAE. Every reported skirmish near Hormuz through May pushed Brent crude higher, and Indian refiners and the finance ministry watched the Strait the way they watch the monsoon: something they cannot control and have to plan the year's budget around anyway. Dubai airport reported a 66 percent drop in March passenger traffic because of the war, a preview of how disruption in one country's airspace cascades through a region India depends on for both energy and expatriate remittances.

By the end of May there was no peace deal, only a war that had not, for the moment, become a full naval blockade. The settlement that eventually stopped it, the Islamabad Memorandum, was still six weeks away.

topics.title: The Supreme Court upholds the Bihar electoral roll purge
topics.hook: On 27 May 2026 the Supreme Court closed the book on the Bihar Special Intensive Revision, ruling that striking 47 lakh names off the rolls before an election was lawful, proportionate and within the Election Commission's power.
topics.story:
The dispute went back to June 2025, when the Election Commission of India ordered a Special Intensive Revision, or SIR, of Bihar's electoral rolls ahead of that year's assembly election. The exercise started with 7.89 crore voters on the rolls. Every voter had to file fresh documents proving citizenship and residence; anyone who did not was struck off. By the time the final roll was published on 30 September 2025, the number had fallen to 7.42 crore, a drop of roughly 47 lakh names in three months.

The Association for Democratic Reforms and other petitioners went to the Supreme Court, arguing that the SIR was really a backdoor citizenship test dressed up as an administrative exercise, that it disproportionately hit the poor, migrant workers and minorities who struggle to produce paperwork on short notice, and that it was too rushed and too close to an election to be fair. The Election Commission's answer was that Article 324 of the Constitution gives it superintendence over elections precisely so it can keep the rolls clean, and that Section 21(3) of the Representation of the People Act, 1950 lets it revise rolls as it sees fit.

A bench led by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, sitting with Justice Joymalya Bagchi, took up the case through 2025 and into 2026, at one point directing the Commission to hand over details of the 3.66 lakh voters excluded from the final roll so their exclusions could be checked. The final judgment came on 27 May 2026, well after the Bihar election itself had already been held and its results declared on 14 November 2025 under the revised rolls.

The Court upheld the SIR as constitutional, procedurally sound and proportionate. It read Article 324 broadly, holding that an intensive revision serves the same purpose the Constitution assigns the Commission: an accurate roll is the precondition for a free and fair election, not an obstacle to one. On the citizenship question, the bench drew a careful line. The Commission can ask about citizenship while compiling rolls, because a non-citizen has no right to vote, but it cannot make a final, binding determination of anyone's citizenship status; that remains the job of the machinery set up under the Citizenship Act, 1955.

For an aspirant this case sits at the intersection of three things CLAT tests constantly: the Election Commission's constitutional status, the limits of executive and quasi-judicial power, and the recurring argument in Indian law over how much process is due before the state can take away a right. The result also carries forward: the same SIR method has since been rolled out to more states, so the Bihar verdict effectively became the template.

topics.title: No fundamental right to bet: the Supreme Court upholds the rummy and poker ban
topics.hook: The Supreme Court ruled on 27 May 2026 that Tamil Nadu and Karnataka can ban online rummy and poker played for money, holding that betting on a game of skill is still gambling, and gambling gets no protection under the right to trade.
topics.story:
Tamil Nadu and Karnataka had each tried, and each been blocked, before this. Tamil Nadu passed the Tamil Nadu Gaming and Police Laws (Amendment) Act, 2021, then a further Online Gambling Act in 2022-23, widening the definition of gaming to catch rummy and poker played online for stakes. The Madras High Court struck the law down. Karnataka's equivalent law met the same fate at its own High Court. Both states argued that money changes the character of a game; both High Courts had held that rummy and poker are games of skill under settled law, and skill games enjoy a level of constitutional protection that pure games of chance do not.

The case, State of Tamil Nadu v. Junglee Games India Pvt. Ltd., reached the Supreme Court on appeal. A bench of Justices J.B. Pardiwala and R. Mahadevan set aside both High Court rulings on 27 May 2026. The Court's reasoning turned the skill-versus-chance question, the one that had decided every previous round of this fight since the 1957 case that first drew the line for rummy, into a side issue. Once real money enters a game, the Court said, its constitutional character changes regardless of how much skill is involved: betting on a game of skill is still a gambling enterprise, and gambling is not a trade or business protected under Article 19(1)(g).

The Court accepted the states' argument that they were regulating a public health and public order problem, not restricting a trade. Both governments had presented data on gaming addiction, suicides linked to online betting losses, and the burden on family courts and police from gambling-related debt. The judgment effectively hands every state government the same tool: as long as a law targets games played for stakes rather than for free, it sits outside the fundamental right to trade and does not need to survive the reasonableness test Article 19(6) would otherwise demand.

The ruling lands at a moment when India's real-money gaming industry, built on fantasy sports, rummy and poker platforms, had grown into a business worth billions of dollars and drawn central-level attention too, with Parliament separately debating a law to regulate or restrict online money games at the national level. States now have Supreme Court cover to move first and move harder, and the ruling is likely to be cited well beyond gaming, in any future case about whether an activity built around stakes can claim the shelter of Article 19(1)(g) at all.

topics.title: India signs 10-year long-term agreement for Chabahar Port operation
topics.hook: India Global Ports Limited (IPGL) signed a 10-year contract with Iran's Ports and Maritime Organisation to equip and operate the Shahid Beheshti Terminal at Chabahar Port.
topics.story:
On 13 May 2026, Union Minister of Ports, Shipping and Waterways Sarbananda Sonowal witnessed the signing of a landmark 10-year long-term bilateral contract in Tehran between India Ports Global Limited (IPGL) and Iran's Ports and Maritime Organization (PMO).

Under the agreement, IPGL will invest approximately $120 million in equipping the Shahid Beheshti terminal at Chabahar Port, alongside a $250 million credit window offered by India for infrastructure expansion. Chabahar, located in the Sistan-Baluchestan province on Iran's southeastern coast, provides India a bypass route to Afghanistan and Central Asia, avoiding Pakistan.

The port forms a key node in the International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC), a 7,200-km multi-modal transit network linking India, Iran, Azerbaijan, and Russia. India's operational involvement in Chabahar counters China's presence at Pakistan's Gwadar port, located just 170 km east along the Gulf of Oman.

The United States State Department issued a caution regarding potential sanctions risks under the Iran Freedom and Counter-Proliferation Act (IFCA), though India maintains Chabahar's strategic exemption granted historically for humanitarian assistance to landlocked Afghanistan.

topics.title: The Supreme Court goes from 34 judges to 38
topics.hook: The Constitution never fixed the number. Parliament has raised it seven times, and the pendency argument has been the same each time.
topics.story:
The Union Cabinet cleared a proposal in May to raise the sanctioned strength of the Supreme Court from **34 judges** to **38**, and the change requires an amendment to the **Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Act, 1956**.

The number has never been in the Constitution. **Article 124(1)** provides for a Chief Justice and such number of other judges as Parliament may by law prescribe, and until Parliament does so the ceiling is seven. Parliament has raised it repeatedly: to 11 in 1956, 14 in 1960, 18 in 1978, 26 in 1986, 31 in 2009 and 34 in 2019. Every increase has been justified on the same ground, that the pendency of cases has outgrown the bench, and every increase has been followed within a few years by the same argument.

The pendency figures do carry the argument some distance. Around **83,000 cases** are pending in the Supreme Court, over **63 lakh** in the High Courts and more than **4.5 crore** in the district judiciary, and the district figure is the one that actually determines how long an ordinary litigant waits. Critics of the increase make two points. Adding judges to the apex court does nothing for the subordinate courts where the backlog sits, and a larger court sitting in more two-judge benches produces more conflicting decisions, which then need larger benches to resolve.

Appointments themselves still run through the **collegium**, the Chief Justice with the four next senior judges, which the Constitution does not mention and which the Court created for itself in the Second and Third Judges cases. The government's attempt to replace it with the **National Judicial Appointments Commission** was struck down in 2015. A higher sanctioned strength therefore enlarges the pool the collegium fills, and changes nothing about who fills it.

topics.title: Emergency medical care read into Article 21
topics.hook: A hospital that turns away a road accident victim for want of paperwork is now refusing a fundamental right, not just breaching an ethical rule.
topics.story:
The Supreme Court held in May that access to **emergency medical care** is part of the right to life under **Article 21**, and directed that no hospital, public or private, may refuse immediate treatment to a person in a medical emergency for want of documentation, police clearance or advance payment.

The holding sits on a line of cases rather than appearing from nowhere. **Parmanand Katara v. Union of India (1989)** had already held that every doctor, whether at a government hospital or in private practice, is obliged to extend medical aid to preserve life, and that no procedural formality may stand in the way. **Paschim Banga Khet Mazdoor Samity v. State of West Bengal (1996)** went further and held the state liable in compensation where a man with head injuries was turned away by several government hospitals for want of beds, because Article 21 obliges the state to provide adequate medical facilities. The Court in 2026 pulled these together and made the obligation enforceable against private hospitals directly rather than through the state.

Article 21 has been the workhorse of Indian rights law for the same reason. **Maneka Gandhi (1978)** required any procedure depriving a person of life or liberty to be fair, just and reasonable, which converted the article from a procedural guarantee into a source of substantive rights. Courts have since read into it a right to livelihood, to a clean environment, to education for children until the Eighty-Sixth Amendment made it explicit in **Article 21A**, to privacy in **Puttaswamy (2017)**, and to die with dignity in **Common Cause (2018)**.

The practical question the judgment leaves open is enforcement. Refusal usually happens in the first minutes at a reception desk, where no court is watching, and the directions rely on state governments framing rules and on hospital licensing conditions carrying the obligation.

topics.title: Assam passes a Uniform Civil Code Bill
topics.hook: Article 44 tells the state to endeavour. It says nothing about which state.
topics.story:
The Assam Assembly passed a **Uniform Civil Code** Bill in May, following **Uttarakhand**, which enacted the first such state code in 2024 and brought it into force in January 2025. A state code covers marriage, divorce, succession, adoption and maintenance, and applies to residents of the state whether or not they live there.

The constitutional basis is **Article 44**, a Directive Principle which says the state shall endeavour to secure for citizens a uniform civil code throughout the territory of India. Directive Principles are, by **Article 37**, not enforceable by any court, but fundamental in the governance of the country. The Constituent Assembly debated the article at length; **Ambedkar** argued that a uniform code was permissive and that no government would force it on an unwilling community, and members from the minority benches pressed unsuccessfully for an explicit consent requirement.

The state route works because personal law sits in **Entry 5 of the Concurrent List**, so both Parliament and a state legislature may legislate on marriage, divorce, adoption and succession. A state Bill touching on matters where a central law already exists needs the **President's assent under Article 254(2)** to prevail within the state. **Goa** is often described as already having a uniform code, though what it has is the **Portuguese Civil Code of 1867**, retained after 1961 and applying with several community-specific exceptions.

The legal arguments run in both directions. Supporters point to **Sarla Mudgal (1995)** and **Shah Bano (1985)**, where the Supreme Court urged the state to act on Article 44. Opponents argue that **Article 25**, freedom of religion, and the protection of tribal customary law are put at risk, which is why the Uttarakhand code exempted Scheduled Tribes and why the same question was raised in Assam, a state with substantial tribal populations under the **Sixth Schedule**.

topics.title: The RBI transfers ₹2.86 lakh crore to the Centre
topics.hook: A central bank does not have shareholders, so what it hands the government every August is not really a dividend, and the size of it is decided by a formula almost nobody reads.
topics.story:
The Reserve Bank's Central Board approved a surplus transfer of about **₹2.86 lakh crore** to the central government for the accounting year, a figure close to the record set the previous year and far above what the Budget had assumed.

The transfer is not a dividend in the corporate sense. Under **Section 47 of the RBI Act, 1934**, whatever remains of the Bank's profits after providing for bad debts, depreciation and staff funds is paid to the central government. The profits come mainly from interest on the Bank's holdings of government securities and foreign assets, from gains on the sale of foreign exchange, and increasingly from the difference between the exchange rate at which dollars were bought and the rate at which they are sold.

How much is retained rather than paid over is governed by an **economic capital framework** recommended by the **Bimal Jalan Committee** in 2019 and revised in 2025. The framework sets a **contingent risk buffer** as a band of the balance sheet size, and the revised version widened that band to **4.5% to 7.5%**. Anything above the chosen level flows to the government. A large transfer therefore reflects both a good year and a decision about how much cushion to keep.

For the Budget the money matters in a specific way. It appears under **non-tax revenue**, alongside dividends from public sector undertakings and spectrum receipts, and a transfer larger than budgeted gives the government room either to spend more or to hold the **fiscal deficit** below target without cutting anything. The recurring criticism is that a government which counts on this line is depending on an outcome it does not control, and that pressing a central bank for larger transfers erodes the independence the buffer is meant to protect.

topics.title: India takes the IORA chair and hosts the Indian Ocean Dialogue
topics.hook: Twenty-three countries around one ocean, and the only rule for joining is a coastline on it.
topics.story:
India assumed the chair of the **Indian Ocean Rim Association** for the **2025-27** term and hosted the tenth **Indian Ocean Dialogue** during the period. IORA was founded in **1997** at Mauritius as the Indian Ocean Rim Association for Regional Cooperation, renamed in 2013, and has its secretariat at **Ebene, Mauritius**. Membership is open to any sovereign state of the Indian Ocean rim; it now has **23 members** and eleven dialogue partners, including China, the United States, Japan and the European Union. **Pakistan** has applied and been blocked, as consensus is required.

The grouping works through six priority areas: maritime safety and security, trade and investment facilitation, fisheries management, disaster risk management, academic and science cooperation, and tourism, with the blue economy and women's economic empowerment added as cross-cutting themes. It has no security function and no standing force, which is both its limitation and the reason a membership this diverse holds together.

India's own framing has moved on. The **SAGAR** doctrine, Security and Growth for All in the Region, announced at Mauritius in 2015, was recast in 2025 as **MAHASAGAR**, Mutual and Holistic Advancement for Security and Growth Across Regions, extending the same idea to Africa and the wider Global South. Alongside it India runs the **Information Fusion Centre for the Indian Ocean Region** at Gurugram, which shares merchant shipping data with partner navies, and the **Colombo Security Conclave** with Sri Lanka, the Maldives, Mauritius and Bangladesh.

The context is competition. Chinese port investment and naval deployment across the ocean, the reopening of the Red Sea route after Houthi attacks disrupted it, and the **India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor** agreed at the 2023 G20 all run through the same water.

topics.title: The EU carbon border tax goes live and India objects
topics.hook: A tariff that calls itself a climate measure, on goods that were never made in Europe.
topics.story:
The European Union's **Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism** entered its definitive phase from **1 January 2026**, after a transitional period from October 2023 in which importers only had to report. From now importers must buy **CBAM certificates** priced against the EU Emissions Trading System to cover the embedded emissions of covered goods, with a deduction for any carbon price already paid in the country of origin.

The covered sectors are **iron and steel, aluminium, cement, fertilisers, electricity and hydrogen**, chosen because they are emissions-intensive and exposed to trade. For India the first two matter most: steel and aluminium make up a large share of what India sells into the EU, and the EU is one of India's largest export markets.

India's objection has three parts. The mechanism is a unilateral trade measure dressed as climate policy, and so sits awkwardly with the **common but differentiated responsibilities** principle written into the UNFCCC and repeated in the Paris Agreement. It discriminates in effect against developing producers whose grids are coal-heavy, since the emissions are measured at the point of production. And it may violate **GATT** rules on national treatment and most favoured nation, an argument India has raised at the WTO Committee on Trade and Environment while stopping short of a formal dispute. India has also said it would consider a **retaliatory levy** if the measure is applied without accommodation, and has pushed the issue into the India-EU free trade negotiations.

The domestic response is a **carbon credit trading scheme** notified under the Energy Conservation (Amendment) Act 2022, with a compliance mechanism for energy-intensive industries. If Indian producers pay a domestic carbon price, that price is deductible against the CBAM certificate cost, which turns a transfer to Brussels into revenue collected at home.

topics.title: India and Vietnam move to the top tier of partnership
topics.hook: India has about thirty strategic partnerships. Only a handful sit at the top of the ladder, and the rungs mean something.
topics.story:
India and Vietnam upgraded their relationship to an **Enhanced Comprehensive Strategic Partnership** in May, with a trade target of about **$25 billion by 2030** and expanded defence and maritime cooperation.

The ladder of Indian partnership labels runs roughly from a plain strategic partnership, through a comprehensive strategic partnership, to the special or enhanced versions reserved for a few. Vietnam had been a **Comprehensive Strategic Partner** since **2016**, one of the first countries in Southeast Asia to reach that level, and the two had already signed a **Joint Vision for Peace, Prosperity and People** in 2020.

Defence is the substance. India extended a **$500 million** defence line of credit, has delivered patrol vessels built at Larsen and Toubro's Kattupalli yard, trains Vietnamese submariners and fighter pilots, and gifted a decommissioned corvette. The **BrahMos** missile has been discussed for years and has been sold to the Philippines, which makes Vietnam the obvious next customer. India's **ONGC Videsh** holds exploration blocks in Vietnamese waters that China's nine-dash line claim overlaps, which is where the two countries' positions on the **South China Sea** converge: both insist on the **UN Convention on the Law of the Sea** and on the 2016 arbitral award that rejected the nine-dash line.

The relationship sits inside **Act East**, which the Look East policy of 1992 became in 2014, and inside the **India-ASEAN** framework where Vietnam has often carried India's case. Vietnam is one of the four ASEAN claimants in the South China Sea, along with the Philippines, Malaysia and Brunei, and its balancing act between Washington and Beijing has made it a useful partner for a country doing something similar.

topics.title: India-UAE trade crosses $100 billion
topics.hook: A trade agreement negotiated in eighty-eight days, and the target it set for 2030 was met four years early.
topics.story:
Bilateral trade between India and the United Arab Emirates crossed **$100 billion**, the target the two countries had set for 2030 when they signed their **Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement**. The agreement was negotiated in about **eighty-eight days**, signed in **February 2022** and in force from **1 May 2022**, and it was India's first trade deal of its kind in a decade.

The CEPA removed tariffs on the large majority of tariff lines, phased over several years, and covers services, government procurement, digital trade and intellectual property. Indian gems and jewellery, textiles, engineering goods and pharmaceuticals gained; the UAE's petroleum products and its role as a re-export hub gained on the other side. The UAE is India's third largest trading partner after the United States and China, and its second largest export destination.

Beyond trade the relationship has three legs. **Energy**: the UAE is a major crude supplier and holds capacity in India's **strategic petroleum reserve** at Mangaluru and Padur, with further agreements on LNG storage. **Payments**: the two central banks agreed in 2023 to settle bilateral trade in rupees and dirhams and to link the **UPI** with the UAE's instant payment platform, which cuts the cost of remittances sent by a diaspora of roughly **3.5 million** Indians, the largest expatriate group in the country. **Connectivity**: the UAE is a signatory to the **India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor** agreed at the G20 in New Delhi in 2023, and the corridor's eastern leg runs from Indian ports to Jebel Ali.

The newer additions are in artificial intelligence infrastructure and data centres, where Emirati sovereign funds have committed capital to Indian projects and Indian firms have taken space in Emirati compute capacity.

topics.title: The essential religious practices doctrine comes back up
topics.hook: A court that decides which parts of a religion are essential is doing theology, and it has been doing it since 1954.
topics.story:
The Supreme Court returned in May to the **essential religious practices** test while dealing with the pending **Sabarimala** review reference, and restated the limit: the doctrine protects only what is essential to a religion, leaving secular activity associated with religion open to state regulation.

The doctrine comes from **Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments v. Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar of Shirur Mutt (1954)**, where the Court held that what constitutes an essential part of a religion is to be decided with reference to the doctrines of that religion itself. In practice courts have decided it themselves, reading scripture and expert evidence, which is the standing criticism: **Article 25** protects freedom of conscience and the right to profess, practise and propagate religion subject to public order, morality, health and the other Part III rights, and **Article 25(2)(a)** expressly allows the state to regulate secular activity associated with religious practice.

The test has produced uneven results. **Ananda Marga** was denied the right to perform the tandava dance in public. Excommunication by the Dai of the Dawoodi Bohras was upheld in 1962 and is again under challenge. In **Shayara Bano (2017)** the majority struck down instant triple talaq without resting on the doctrine, while one opinion held it was not an essential practice. In **Indian Young Lawyers Association (2018)** a majority held the exclusion of women of menstruating age from Sabarimala was not an essential practice and violated Articles 25 and 14. The **2019 review** did not decide the case; it referred a set of broader questions on the interplay of religious freedom, equality and constitutional morality to a nine-judge bench, which has not yet ruled.

topics.hook: Two numbers released within days of each other, measured by two different offices, and only one of them is easy to argue about.
topics.story:
The **National Statistics Office** put growth for the fourth quarter of **2025-26** at about **7.2%**, keeping India the fastest growing major economy. Quarterly estimates come from the NSO under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation, which issues advance estimates in January, provisional estimates in May and revisions afterwards; the base year for the series is **2011-12**, with a revision to 2022-23 under way.

The **Periodic Labour Force Survey**, run by the same ministry, reported unemployment at about **5%**. PLFS has been monthly for urban areas and now reports rural figures monthly too, and it measures on two definitions: **usual status**, over a year, and **current weekly status**, over the preceding week. The survey also showed rural workers moving out of agriculture towards manufacturing and services.

The two numbers are read together because the standing criticism of Indian growth is that it has not produced proportionate employment. Growth is measured by value added, which rises fastest in capital-intensive sectors, while employment sits in construction, agriculture and small trade.

topics.title: The GST Council cuts rates on EV batteries and medical devices
topics.hook: The one constitutional body where the Centre holds a third of the votes and can still be outvoted, in theory.
topics.story:
The **GST Council** reduced rates on **electric vehicle batteries** and on a set of **medical devices**, both moves aimed at adoption rather than revenue.

The Council is a constitutional body created by **Article 279A**, inserted by the **101st Amendment** in 2016. It is chaired by the **Union Finance Minister**, with the Minister of State for Finance and one minister from each state. Decisions need a **three-fourths majority** of weighted votes; the Centre holds **one-third** of the total and the states together **two-thirds**, so neither side can act alone. Quorum is half the members.

Its recommendations were long treated as binding in practice. In **Mohit Minerals (2022)**, dealing with integrated GST on ocean freight, the Supreme Court held that the Council's recommendations are **persuasive and not binding**, since both Parliament and state legislatures have simultaneous power to legislate on GST. The finding unsettled the assumption that the Council speaks with a single enforceable voice, though in practice its decisions are still adopted.

topics.title: The Asiatic lion count reaches 891
topics.hook: Every Asiatic lion alive is descended from a population that dropped to perhaps twenty animals in one forest in Gujarat.
topics.story:
The Gujarat forest department's estimation put the **Asiatic lion** population at **891**, up from 674 at the previous count in 2020. The lion survives in the wild only in and around the **Gir** forest in Saurashtra, and more than half the population now lives outside the protected area, in farmland, coastal scrub and near the Girnar hills.

The species is **Panthera leo persica**, listed as **Endangered** by the IUCN and placed in the highest protection schedule of the **Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972**. **Project Lion** was announced in 2020, along the lines of Project Tiger, and the state runs the count on a block-by-block direct sighting method rather than by camera trap.

Concentration in one place is the risk. The **canine distemper virus** killed dozens of lions in 2018 and the same disease nearly wiped out the Serengeti population in 1994. The Supreme Court ordered in **2013** that some lions be translocated to **Kuno** in Madhya Pradesh; Gujarat did not comply, and Kuno was later used for the African cheetah introduction instead.

topics.title: DRDO tests a glide weapon and an Agni-5 variant
topics.hook: A missile that splits into several warheads on separate paths is one weapon on paper and several problems for an interceptor.
topics.story:
The Defence Research and Development Organisation tested **TARA**, described as India's first indigenous precision glide weapon, and a variant of the **Agni-5** intermediate range ballistic missile.

A glide weapon is released from an aircraft and glides to the target without an engine, guided by satellite and inertial navigation, which lets the launch aircraft stay outside air defence range. India already fields the **SAAW** and the **Gaurav** long-range glide bomb in this class.

**Agni-5** has a range beyond 5,000 km and was first tested with **MIRV** capability in **Mission Divyastra** in March 2024. MIRV, or multiple independently targetable re-entry vehicles, lets one missile carry several warheads aimed at separate targets, which complicates missile defence and is why only a handful of countries have demonstrated it. India's declared nuclear posture remains **credible minimum deterrence** with **no first use**, set out after the 1998 Pokhran-II tests and formalised in the 2003 doctrine, which reserves the right to retaliate massively and also to respond to a chemical or biological attack.

Defence production reached about **₹1.54 lakh crore** in 2024-25, with exports rising sharply from a low base.

topics.title: Cristian Mungiu wins a second Palme d'Or
topics.hook: Only ten directors have won the Palme d'Or twice, and the tenth did it nineteen years after the first.
topics.story:
**Fjord**, directed by the Romanian **Cristian Mungiu** and starring Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve, won the **Palme d'Or** at the **79th Festival de Cannes**, which closed on 23 May 2026. Mungiu had won in 2007 for **4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days**, and becomes the tenth director to take the prize twice.

Cannes has run since **1946** and awards the Palme d'Or for the best film in competition, with the **Grand Prix** as the runner-up prize and the **Jury Prize** below it. The Indian record at the festival is short: **Chetan Anand's Neecha Nagar** shared the top prize at the first edition in 1946, **Payal Kapadia's All We Imagine as Light** took the Grand Prix in 2024, and the same director had won the Golden Eye documentary prize in 2021.

Cannes sits alongside **Berlin**, which awards the Golden Bear, and **Venice**, the oldest of the three, which awards the Golden Lion.

topics.title: World Migration Report 2026: India leads on diaspora and remittances
topics.hook: The largest flow of money into India from abroad is not investment. It is people sending money home.
topics.story:
The **World Migration Report 2026**, published by the **International Organization for Migration**, confirmed India as the country with the **largest diaspora** and the **largest recipient of remittances**. Indian remittance receipts have been above **$100 billion** a year since 2022, ahead of Mexico and China, and exceed India's annual foreign direct investment inflows. The largest sources are the United States, the United Arab Emirates and the other Gulf states.

IOM was founded in 1951 and became a **related organisation of the United Nations** in 2016, joining the UN system without becoming a specialised agency. The report also recorded that climate-related disasters triggered millions of internal displacements, a category counted separately from cross-border migration and dominated by South Asia and East Asia.

India's own framework distinguishes **non-resident Indians**, who are citizens, from **Overseas Citizens of India**, a status created in 2005 that gives lifelong visa-free entry and most economic rights but no vote and no public office. Dual citizenship is not permitted.

topics.title: Deep-sea mining and the authority nobody wants to obey
topics.hook: The seabed beyond national jurisdiction is legally the common heritage of mankind, which is a strong phrase with a weak enforcement mechanism.
topics.story:
Demand for battery metals has revived interest in mining polymetallic nodules from the deep ocean floor, and the **International Seabed Authority** criticised United States efforts to fast-track permits outside its process.

The Authority was created by the **UN Convention on the Law of the Sea**, which came into force in 1994, and administers the **Area**, the seabed beyond national jurisdiction, declared the **common heritage of mankind**. It has issued exploration contracts but has not finalised the exploitation regulations, the so-called mining code, and several states have called for a moratorium until the ecological effects are understood. The **United States has not ratified UNCLOS**, which is the gap the fast-track permits exploit.

India holds exploration rights over about **75,000 sq km** in the **Central Indian Ocean Basin** for polymetallic nodules and a further area on the **Carlsberg Ridge** for sulphides. The **Deep Ocean Mission**, approved in 2021, includes **Samudrayaan**, a crewed submersible called **Matsya-6000** designed to reach 6,000 metres.

topics.title: The Global Forest Goals Report counts the loss
topics.hook: The world agreed in 2015 to increase forest area. Ten years on, forty million hectares had gone the other way.
topics.story:
The **Global Forest Goals Report 2026**, published under the **United Nations Forum on Forests**, recorded a loss of more than **40 million hectares** of forest between 2015 and 2025, driven by agricultural expansion, climate change, wildfires and illegal logging. The Forum sits under the Economic and Social Council and oversees the **UN Strategic Plan for Forests 2017-2030**, whose first goal is to reverse forest loss.

Forest data in India comes from the **India State of Forest Report**, published every two years by the **Forest Survey of India** at Dehradun. India reports forest and tree cover at roughly a quarter of its area, against a **National Forest Policy 1988** target of a third, and the count is contested because plantations and orchards are included in what is measured from satellite.

The governing statutes are the **Forest (Conservation) Act 1980**, renamed the Van Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan Adhiniyam in 2023, and the **Forest Rights Act 2006**, which recognises individual and community rights of forest-dwelling Scheduled Tribes and other traditional forest dwellers.

passages.title: The right that keeps growing
passages.passage:
The provision runs to a single sentence and says only that no person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law. For the first twenty-eight years it was read narrowly, and a majority of the Court held during the Emergency that even the right to move a court for enforcement could be suspended. The turn came in 1978, when the Court held that the procedure contemplated by the article could not be any procedure a legislature chose to enact, but had to be fair, just and reasonable. That reading converted a procedural safeguard into a source of substantive entitlements, and the entitlements have accumulated ever since.

Some were recognised early. A person who is arrested has to be told why, has to be produced before a magistrate, and cannot be kept in solitary confinement or in fetters as a matter of routine. A pavement dweller evicted without notice was held to lose a right to livelihood that the article protected, because a person deprived of the means of living is deprived of life itself. Later cases added a clean environment, a speedy trial, legal aid, shelter, and education for children, the last of which Parliament eventually wrote into a separate article of its own.

The recent additions have run into private conduct. In May 2026 the Court held that a person in a medical emergency has a right to immediate treatment that binds private hospitals directly, not merely the state, and that no formality of documentation or payment may stand in the way. Two earlier judgments had pointed there: one in 1989 holding that a doctor's obligation to preserve life admits of no procedural excuse, and one in 1996 awarding compensation where a man with head injuries was turned away by a series of state hospitals.

questions.q: The provision described is:
questions.explain: Article 21, life and personal liberty.

questions.q: The 1978 decision that changed its reading is:
questions.explain: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India held that the procedure must be fair, just and reasonable.

questions.q: The right to education for children was later placed in:
questions.explain: Article 21A, inserted by the 86th Amendment in 2002.

questions.q: On the passage, what is new about the May 2026 ruling?
options: It created a right to health for the first time
It applied only to government hospitals
It made treatment free of cost
questions.explain: The passage says the obligation binds private hospitals directly rather than through the state.

questions.q: The 1996 judgment referred to awarded:
questions.explain: Paschim Banga Khet Mazdoor Samity awarded compensation for the denial of emergency treatment.

passages.title: A tariff by another name
passages.passage:
From the start of 2026 an importer bringing steel, aluminium, cement, fertiliser, electricity or hydrogen into the European Union has had to buy certificates covering the greenhouse gases emitted in making those goods, priced against the bloc's own carbon market. A transitional phase from late 2023 had required only that the emissions be reported. Any carbon price already paid where the goods were produced is deducted from what the importer owes.

The stated purpose is to stop carbon leakage, the movement of emissions-intensive production to countries with looser rules, which would leave the bloc's own industry undercut and the atmosphere no better off. The objection from developing exporters is that the measure is unilateral, that it was designed without their participation, and that it sits badly with a principle written into the climate convention of 1992 and repeated since: that states share a responsibility for the climate but not an equal one, given their different historical contributions and different capacities.

There is also a trade law argument, that a charge calculated on the production method rather than on the product itself may fall foul of the rules on national treatment and most favoured nation. India has raised the point in a WTO committee without filing a formal dispute, and has said it would consider a countervailing levy of its own.

The more interesting response has been domestic. If a producer pays a carbon price at home, that payment reduces the certificate cost at the border. A country that taxes its own emissions therefore keeps the revenue that would otherwise cross to Brussels, which is an argument for a domestic carbon market made entirely on grounds of national self-interest.

options: All imports into the European Union
questions.explain: Iron and steel, aluminium, cement, fertiliser, electricity and hydrogen.

questions.q: The principle the objection rests on is:
questions.explain: Common but differentiated responsibilities, from the 1992 UNFCCC.

questions.q: The stated purpose of the measure is to prevent:
questions.explain: Carbon leakage, the shifting of emissions-intensive production to laxer jurisdictions.

options: It exempts exports from the mechanism entirely
It reduces the certificate cost and keeps the revenue at home
It lowers the European carbon price
questions.explain: The deduction means the money is collected at home instead of at the European border.

options: The production method rather than the product

passages.title: Counting judges
passages.passage:
The number is not in the Constitution. The relevant article provides for a Chief Justice and such number of other judges as Parliament may by law prescribe, and fixes a floor of seven until Parliament acts. The court opened in 1950 with eight judges including the Chief Justice, and Parliament has legislated seven times since to raise the ceiling, most recently to thirty-four in 2019 and now to thirty-eight.

Each increase has been justified on the same ground and followed by the same result. The argument is arrears; the counter-argument, made every time, is that the arrears are not at the top. Something like eighty thousand matters are pending before the apex court, over sixty lakh before the High Courts, and more than four and a half crore before the district judiciary, where an ordinary litigant actually waits. Adding four judges to a court that already sits mostly in benches of two also multiplies the number of two-judge decisions, which multiplies conflicts between them, which produces references to larger benches, which is itself a source of delay.

Nothing in the change touches how the judges arrive. That process is not in the Constitution either. The text says appointments are made by the President after consultation with such judges as he considers necessary, and for decades consultation meant what it says. Three decisions between 1981 and 1998 converted consultation into concurrence and then into a recommendation by the Chief Justice acting with a plurality of senior colleagues, an arrangement the Constitution nowhere describes. Parliament tried to replace it in 2014 with a commission including the Law Minister and two eminent persons; a five-judge bench struck down both the amendment and the Act the following year, holding that the primacy of the judiciary in appointments is part of the basic structure.

What remains is a memorandum of procedure the two sides have never finalised, a recurring quarrel about names returned and resent, and now four more vacancies to fill by the same route.

questions.explain: Article 124(1) provides for a Chief Justice and seven other judges until Parliament prescribes more.

options: The backlog is in the lower courts, not the apex court
questions.explain: The passage locates the real backlog in the district judiciary.

questions.explain: The First, Second and Third Judges cases, which created the collegium.

questions.explain: The NJAC, established by the 99th Amendment and struck down in 2015.

questions.explain: The Fourth Judges case held judicial primacy in appointments to be a basic feature.

passages.title: An endeavour, not a command
passages.passage:
The provision is one sentence long and sits in the part of the Constitution that courts may not enforce. It says the state shall endeavour to secure for the citizens a uniform civil code throughout the territory of India. The Constituent Assembly debated it for a day. Members from the minority benches moved amendments requiring the prior consent of the communities affected; the amendments were defeated, but the chairman of the drafting committee told the House in reply that the article was permissive, that it merely gave the state power it might never exercise, and that no future government would be so unwise as to impose a code on an unwilling population.

Seventy-five years later two state legislatures have done what the Union has not. The route is a matter of legislative lists: personal law, including marriage, divorce, infants and minors, adoption, wills, intestacy and succession, appears in the concurrent list, so a state may legislate on it. Where a state law conflicts with an existing central law, it prevails within that state if it has been reserved for and received the assent of the President.

The state that went first exempted its scheduled tribes, and the second faced the same question in a sharper form, having a substantial population governed by customary law under a schedule of the Constitution that gives autonomous district councils power over marriage and inheritance among themselves.

The argument for is judicial. Courts have twice pressed the point in maintenance and conversion cases, observing that a common code would help national integration and remove contradictions based on conflicting ideologies. The argument against rests on the freedom to profess and practise religion, and on the observation that the one territory often described as already having such a code inherited it from a colonial power in 1867 and applies it with several community-specific exceptions, which makes it a poor advertisement for uniformity.

questions.explain: Article 44, a Directive Principle of State Policy.

questions.q: The chairman of the drafting committee who replied in the debate was:
questions.explain: Ambedkar chaired the drafting committee and answered the amendments on Article 44.

questions.q: A state may legislate on personal law because it appears in the:
questions.explain: Entry 5 of the Concurrent List covers marriage, divorce, adoption and succession.

options: It is passed by a two-thirds majority

options: Has a modern uniform code applying to all

questions.explain: Goa applies the Portuguese Civil Code of 1867 with several exceptions.

passages.title: What a central bank does with its profit
passages.passage:
It is routinely called a dividend and it is not one. A central bank has no shareholders in the ordinary sense; the governing statute of 1934 simply provides that after making provision for bad and doubtful debts, depreciation in assets, contributions to staff and superannuation funds and all other matters for which provision is customarily made, the balance of the profits shall be paid to the central government.

The profits come from three places. The bank holds a large portfolio of government securities and earns interest on them. It holds foreign assets and earns a return on those. And it buys and sells foreign currency in the market, booking the difference between the historical rate at which the dollars were acquired and the rate at which they are sold, which in a year of heavy intervention can be the largest single item.

How much is retained rather than paid over is not left to discretion. A committee that reported in 2019 recommended a framework under which the bank holds a contingent risk buffer within a band expressed as a percentage of its balance sheet, to absorb monetary and financial stability risks; the framework was revised in 2025 and the band widened. Whatever sits above the level chosen within that band flows to the government. A large transfer therefore reflects two separate things: a profitable year, and a decision about how much cushion to keep.

For the budget the money appears under non-tax revenue, alongside dividends from public sector undertakings and receipts from spectrum. A transfer above what was assumed gives the government room to spend more or to hold the deficit below target without cutting anything, which is why the figure is watched. The standing objection is that a government which builds its arithmetic around this line becomes interested in how large the buffer is, and a central bank whose cushion is set by someone with an interest in it being small has a problem it cannot solve with monetary policy.

questions.q: The transfer is made under:
questions.explain: Section 47 provides for surplus profits to be paid to the central government.

questions.q: Which is NOT given in the passage as a source of the bank's profits?
questions.explain: The passage lists the first three only.

questions.q: The 2019 committee recommended a framework centred on:
options: A contingent risk buffer as a band of the balance sheet
A cap on foreign exchange reserves
questions.explain: The economic capital framework recommended by the Bimal Jalan Committee.

questions.q: In the Union Budget the transfer appears as:
questions.explain: Non-tax revenue, with PSU dividends and spectrum receipts.

questions.q: The objection stated in the last paragraph is essentially about:
questions.explain: That a government dependent on the transfer acquires an interest in the size of the buffer.

passages.title: An association with no teeth, on purpose
passages.passage:
Twenty-three states sit around one ocean and belong to a body founded in 1997 on a Mauritian initiative, with a secretariat on that island. The only qualification for membership is a coastline on the ocean in question, which is why the membership includes states at war with each other's allies, states of wildly different size, and states with almost nothing in common beyond salt water. One applicant has been kept out for two decades because admission requires consensus and one member will not give it.

The body works through six priority areas: maritime safety and security, trade and investment facilitation, fisheries management, disaster risk management, academic and scientific cooperation, and tourism, with the blue economy and women's economic empowerment running across all of them. It has no security function, no standing force, and no dispute mechanism. That is usually described as a weakness; it is at least as accurate to call it the condition on which a membership this heterogeneous holds together at all.

India took the rotating chair for the 2025 to 2027 term. Its own framing of the region has moved twice. A doctrine announced at Mauritius in 2015 gave the acronym for security and growth for all in the region, and was recast a decade later under a longer name extending the same idea to Africa and the wider global south. Alongside it India runs a fusion centre near Delhi that shares merchant shipping tracks with partner navies, and a five-country security conclave with its immediate maritime neighbours.

The context is competition it cannot name in a communiqué. Port investment and naval deployment by a state that is only a dialogue partner, the disruption and partial reopening of the Red Sea route, and a corridor agreed at a summit in New Delhi in 2023 that would run from Indian ports through the Gulf to Europe all cross the same water, and none of them are on the agenda of the six priority areas.

questions.explain: The Indian Ocean Rim Association was founded in 1997, with its secretariat in Mauritius.

questions.explain: Any sovereign state of the Indian Ocean rim may apply.

questions.explain: The passage explicitly reframes the weakness as an enabling condition.

questions.explain: SAGAR, announced at Mauritius in 2015, recast as MAHASAGAR in 2025.

questions.explain: IMEC, agreed at the G20 summit in New Delhi.

passages.title: Judges deciding what a religion requires
passages.passage:
The test was invented in 1954, in a case about a mutt in the Madras presidency whose head objected to a statute placing its endowments under a government commissioner. The court held that what constitutes an essential part of a religion is to be ascertained with reference to the doctrines of that religion itself, and that the protection extends to practices as much as to belief. The sentence has been quoted ever since. What has happened in practice is the opposite of what it says: courts, not communities, decide, and they do it by reading scripture, hearing experts and forming a view about which observances a faith could survive the loss of.

The constitutional text invites some of this. The article guarantees freedom of conscience and the right to profess, practise and propagate religion, but subjects it to public order, morality, health and the other fundamental rights, and then expressly saves any law regulating or restricting economic, financial, political or other secular activity associated with religious practice. Something has to distinguish the religious core from the secular shell, and the test is what the court reached for.

The results have been uneven. A sect was refused the right to perform a dance with skulls in public processions. The power of a religious head to excommunicate was upheld in 1962 and is under challenge again. A ban on a form of unilateral divorce was struck down in 2017, with the plurality avoiding the test and one opinion resting on it. And in 2018 a majority held that excluding women of a particular age group from a temple was not essential to the faith and violated the guarantees of religious freedom and equality alike.

That last judgment was not overruled by what followed. A review in 2019 declined to decide the case and instead referred a set of broader questions — about the interplay of religious freedom with equality, about constitutional morality, about whether a court should be deciding any of this — to a bench of nine judges. Seven years on, those questions have not been answered, and every case in the area is argued in their shadow.

questions.q: The 1954 case that produced the test concerned:
options: A mutt whose endowments were placed under a commissioner
questions.explain: Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments v. Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar of Shirur Mutt.

questions.q: The article guaranteeing freedom of religion also permits the state to regulate:
options: Secular activity associated with religious practice
questions.explain: Article 25(2)(a) saves laws regulating economic, financial, political or other secular activity.

questions.q: On the passage, the standing criticism of the test is that:
options: Courts rather than communities end up deciding what is essential
It cannot be applied to new religions
questions.explain: The passage says practice has inverted what the 1954 sentence prescribed.

questions.q: The 2019 review of the 2018 temple judgment:
options: Referred broader questions to a nine-judge bench
Dismissed the review as not maintainable
questions.explain: It referred questions onward without deciding the case.

questions.q: The 2018 judgment held the exclusion violated:
questions.explain: The majority found breaches of Articles 25 and 14.
